messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 34
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Delivery Driver
- Trauma Type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
- Pcl5: 46

**Vignette: Rajan, Age 34**

Rajan has been driving delivery routes for the same logistics company for six years. He knows the streets of his city the way most people know their own neighborhood — intuitively, almost without thinking. That familiarity is part of what makes what happened eighteen months ago so difficult for him to reconcile. He was doing everything right. He has told himself this hundreds of times, and he still cannot make it feel true.

It was a Tuesday morning in late autumn, a route he had driven dozens of times. A twelve-year-old boy ran from between two parked cars directly into the path of Rajan's van. Rajan braked hard, but not hard enough. The impact was slight by mechanical standards — the boy was struck at low speed — but the child suffered a fractured pelvis and spent three weeks in hospital. He survived. He recovered. Everyone has told Rajan this, as if the outcome should close the matter. For Rajan, it has not closed anything.

In the immediate aftermath, he sat on the pavement beside the van while someone else called for an ambulance. He remembers the sound of the boy crying and the particular gray of the sky that morning, and he remembers his own hands, which would not stop shaking. The police investigation found no fault on his part. His employer kept him on. His wife, Priya, held him that night and told him it was not his fault. He nodded and said he knew, and he did not sleep.

In the months that followed, Rajan returned to work because the family needed the income and because he did not know what else to do with himself. Every shift is an act of endurance. He grips the steering wheel with both hands even on empty roads. When a pedestrian steps off a curb ahead of him, his foot moves to the brake before his mind has consciously registered the movement. He scans constantly — children especially, children near parked cars, children on bikes — and the vigilance exhausts him in a way that sleep does not repair. Several times he has had to pull over and sit for a few minutes, breathing, before he could continue.

At night the images return without invitation. He sees the boy's body against the front of the van. He sees his own hands on the wheel. Sometimes he wakes at two or three in the morning with his heart already racing, the dream dissolving but the feeling staying with him for an hour or more. Priya has begun sleeping lightly because of his restlessness, and Rajan carries guilt about this too — the sense that he is spreading damage outward, that the accident is still injuring people through him.

He has become quieter in general. His younger brother has commented on it. At family gatherings he sits at the edge of conversations, present but not quite reachable. He used to enjoy cooking on weekends, something he and Priya did together; he has largely stopped initiating it. Small pleasures have gone flat in a way he struggles to articulate. He does not think of himself as depressed — he goes to work, he functions, he loves his wife — but he recognizes that something in him is running on a reduced register.

What troubles Rajan most, in the quiet moments he allows himself to examine it, is the question of what kind of person he is now. He was raised in a household where responsibility was taken seriously, where causing harm — even accidentally — carried moral weight. He cannot fully accept the verdict of the investigation or the reassurances of the people who love him. The boy healed. Rajan is still, in some interior way, sitting on that pavement in the gray autumn light, waiting for something he cannot name.
